1987.blurb: By 1987 Alex Chilton had been rediscovered twice — first when Big Star's records surfaced in the late 1970s as a secret history of power pop, and again when the Replacements released "Alex Chilton" that February, a song that named him as a patron saint to a generation who'd never heard the Box Tops. The Cubby Bear on Clark Street, an 800-cap sports bar that doubled as a concert room, is where he played that October and again in December. Chilton's live shows in this period were famously unpredictable — he might play Box Tops hits, Big Star deep cuts, or novelty covers, depending on his mood, and the set list was never announced in advance.

1990.blurb: The Replacements song had changed Chilton's relationship to his own audience. He was still playing Lounge Ax — two shows in the archive, November 1990 and January 1992 — but the room had shifted. Some of the people there had grown up with the Box Tops; more of them had come through the Replacements or through Big Star's third record, *Sister Lovers*, which was being re-released and discussed seriously for the first time. Chilton navigated this without much apparent effort to manage it. He showed up, played what he wanted to play, and left. The mythology around him was not something he cultivated.

Out of Chapel Hill, where Superchunk and Polvo were already running the same playbook, they worked the indie circuit hard: the Middle East in Cambridge, Lounge Ax in Chicago three times in nine months, college towns, 300-cap rooms where you either won the room or you didn't. 1988.blurb: David Grubbs had come north from Louisville and Squirrel Bait, settling in Chicago where Bastro formed around him with Bundy K. Brown on bass and eventually John McEntire on drums. Four albums on Homestead and Touch and Go across four years, all of it played at full volume. The archive catches them across three Chicago rooms in four years: Cubby Bear on Clark, the Czar Bar on Sheffield, Lounge Ax on Lincoln — the Chicago circuit for a band too abrasive for mainstream college radio but too disciplined for the noise underground. Grubbs left a University of Chicago PhD program to tour Europe in 1991; the chair of the English department told him it wouldn't work. By the end of 1991 Bastro had become Gastr del Sol, and McEntire was moving toward what would become Tortoise.

1994.blurb: Bedhead were from Dallas — Matt and Bubba Kadane, plus three others — making slow, quiet, introspective guitar rock on Trance Syndicate, the Austin label that also ran Roky Erickson's catalog. Three Lounge Ax shows: two consecutive nights in May 1994, one in April 1995. The music was deliberate and unhurried, which is not the natural register for touring, but Bedhead toured like they played — on their own terms.

The Reckless Records in-store in March was the kind of thing that happened when a band had enough Matador credibility to get on the college radio playlists but not enough draw to fill a 500-cap room — you did the in-store first, you built the audience, you played the room later.

1997.blurb: *Dust Bunnies* (1997) was Bettie Serveert's third album, made after their US distribution deal with Matador had wound down. The May 1997 Metro show — 1,100 capacity on Clark Street — was the kind of room a band could play when four years of American touring had built a reliable audience in the right cities. Chicago was one of those cities. The band remained Dutch, remained independent, and toured the US less frequently as the decade went on; the Metro shows from this period capture the moment before the audience thinned and the visits became rarer.

2003.blurb: Ten years on from the Reckless Records in-store, Bettie Serveert was playing the Abbey Pub on Chicago's northwest side. The trajectory from Matador in-store to Metro to Abbey Pub is not a story of failure — the Abbey Pub was a good room for a band with a loyal audience that had grown up and didn't need a 1,000-cap venue to feel like the show mattered. *Log 22* (2003) was their fifth record; the Excelsior label was Dutch. They had largely decoupled from the American indie infrastructure and were making records on their own terms with the audience they had built.

1989.blurb: *Bug* came out in October 1988 on SST and the tour that followed it was the last time the original three-piece — J Mascis, Lou Barlow, Murph — would play together for twenty years. The March 25 Cabaret Metro show lands in the middle of that final run. Mascis later said *Bug* was "a bad time," the band already falling apart even as the songs were getting sharper. The volume on stage was the loudest it had been; the relationship offstage was the worst it had been. Barlow was fired somewhere in the middle of 1989. The Metro show is one of the last documented performances of the lineup that made the band.

1993.blurb: By April 1993, Dinosaur Jr. was a different band in a different room. *Where You Been* was on Sire, J Mascis was the sole original member still performing under the name, and the April 10 show was at the Riviera Theatre — 2,500 capacity on Broadway, a venue that booked arena-bound acts between arena tours. The distance between the 1989 Cabaret Metro show and this one was more than the four years between them. The SST budget and the three-piece arrangement were gone; the major label deal and the full-production show had replaced them. Mascis's guitar volume remained the constant.

2012.blurb: Dinosaur Jr. reunited in 2005 with the original lineup — Mascis, Barlow, Murph — and had been making records together since *Beyond* (2007). By June 2012, with *I Bet on Sky* arriving in September, they were playing Subterranean on North Wicker Park Avenue: two nights, the same small stage where unknown bands played their first Chicago shows. The capacity is around 200. That a reunited Dinosaur Jr. was playing a 200-person room in 2012 is either a commentary on where reunion tours go or a deliberate choice to play close — probably the latter, given how much they'd always preferred the floor to the balcony.

Schubas on March 13 — 150 capacity — was the right room: intimate enough that the songs could land as the quiet, domestic things they were, small enough that Barlow could fill it on his own name without the Sebadoh pull. 2012.blurb: The August 2012 Schubas show comes at a moment when Barlow was running multiple tracks simultaneously: Sebadoh was recording *Defend Yourself*, Dinosaur Jr. had been reunited for years, and he was touring solo in between. Schubas again — the same 150-cap room as 2005, the same neighborhood on Belmont, seven years later. The continuity is meaningful: Barlow had never grown out of the room, and the room had never grown past what it was. The audience that came to Schubas for a Lou Barlow solo show in 2012 was the audience that had always been there.

1985.blurb: New Order in 1985 were still a band in transition — three years on from Joy Division and Ian Curtis's death, still playing bass lines that Bernard Sumner had originally written for a different singer, still figuring out what it meant to be a dance band that had come from a post-punk one. The Bismarck Theatre in Chicago — the room that would later become the Vic — sat 1,400 people. Four Chicago shows between 1985 and 1987 charts the band moving through their most prolific period: *Low-Life*, *Brotherhood*, *Substance*, all three years. The shows were notoriously austere — minimal stage production, the band facing forward, the music doing all the work.

Four shows at the Blind Pig — a 400-cap bar on North Halsted — in six days in June. That density is less a strategy than a product of what touring looked like when your label was Matador and your budget was close to nothing: you played the rooms that would book you, you played them back-to-back because you couldn't afford to not be earning, and the audience found you the same way you'd found them. 1997.blurb: By February 1997, *Brighten the Corners* and the Matador years had made Pavement a band that could fill the Double Door twice in a weekend. The room on Milwaukee Avenue held around 500 people — a real step from the Blind Pig four-night stand in 1992. The band was also more settled as a live unit, the lineup having been stable for several years, the chaos of the early tours replaced by something that looked more like a working band. The songs on *Brighten the Corners* were the most immediately accessible they'd made; the shows ran smooth. The breakup would come in 1999.

2003.blurb: The Clean were the Kilgour brothers' band from Dunedin, one of the original Flying Nun groups, and by 2003 they were twenty years into a stop-start existence that had involved long gaps, reunions, solo projects, and occasional records that reminded anyone who'd forgotten what the Dunedin Sound meant in its original context. The Vic Theatre on Sheffield — 1,400 seats, the room that had been the Bismarck when New Order played it in 1985 — was a significant Chicago stage for a New Zealand band with a devoted but niche following. *Getaway* (2001) had been well-received; the June show caught them in one of their more active touring periods.

2010.blurb: *Mister Pop* (2009) was The Clean's first album on Merge Records and their first record in eight years. The September 2010 Bottom Lounge show — a 450-cap room at Lake and Aberdeen on the West Loop — came near the end of the *Mister Pop* touring cycle. Merge distribution meant a different kind of American support than Flying Nun had provided in the 1980s and 1990s; the band's reach was wider, the shows better booked. 2014.blurb: The August 2014 Lincoln Hall show — 500 capacity on North Clark, a proper seated-and-standing concert room — came during a period when Flying Nun was reissuing much of their back catalog and The Clean's historical importance to underground pop was being reassessed by a new generation. Lincoln Hall is where bands go when they have enough of a Chicago audience to need a real venue but not enough for the Metro. For a New Zealand band that had been around since 1978, playing Chicago on a Tuesday night in August in front of five hundred people who all knew every song was exactly the right scale.
